content.text: How do the words characters say help move the story forward?
By noticing and sharing small moments, people build empathy, voice, and community.
Lesson 16 continues to focus on characters’ points of view and how the author develops them.
The unit performance task will require consideration of how dialogue reveals specific information that narration may not.
Look Both Ways
, by Jason Reynolds
Unit 1 Lesson 15 Student Edition
3 Column Chart graphic organizer

Analyze how dialogue helps reveal character traits, points of view, and relationships between characters throughout Vignette 6 of the anchor text, “Five Things Easier to Do Than Simeon’s and Kenzi’s Handshake.”
Explain how dialogue reveals relationships by identifying explicit and implicit meanings, using inference verbs (
implies
suggests
), and citing quoted evidence to justify your interpretation.
Read out loud while paying attention to prosody clues in order to examine explicit versus implicit meanings.

Students will analyze how dialogue helps reveal character traits, points of view, and relationships between characters throughout Vignette 6 of the anchor text, “Five Things Easier to Do Than Simeon’s and Kenzi’s Handshake.”
Students will explain how dialogue reveals relationships by identifying explicit and implicit meanings, using inference verbs (
implies
suggests
), and citing quoted evidence to justify their interpretation.
Students will read out loud while paying attention to prosody clues in order to examine explicit versus implicit meanings.
Language Study
Jigsaw Reading
Directions:
Look at the following dialogue samples for Vignette 6. We are going to discuss whether the samples are informative, entertaining, or both.
“Fantana banana, what’s good? What’s hood? What’s new? What’s true?”
“Anyway, like I was saying. We family.”
“To your mother’s house. Ask her how many times she dropped you when you were a baby.”
Is the first dialogue sample informational, entertaining, or both? Tell us why.
Language Study
Target Words:
explicit, implicit
Where have you seen the words
explicit
and
implicit
before? Do you remember how they are related?
Directions:
Explicit
and
implicit
are opposites.
Explicit
means “made clear with no room for confusion,” and
implicit

means “only implied or suggested.” Today, when we talk about the explicit and implicit meanings of words or phrases, we’re talking about what the exact words mean versus what they might imply in the context of this story.

Remember the context here: Kenzi was riding on Simeon’s back in the hallway. Ms. Wockley caught them, and they said they weren’t pretending to be in a horse race. What is the explicit meaning of what she says to them?
What is the implicit meaning of what Ms. Wockley said?
Why would an author choose to use dialogue that is more implicit?
Part A: Explicit and Implicit Meanings in Dialogue:
Look Both Ways
, Vignette 6
Directions:

In this part, we will continue to analyze the dialogue between Simeon, Kenzi, and Ms. Wockley, teasing apart explicit and implicit meanings to understand how stories help us see through someone else’s eyes.
“See here’s the thing, Wockley Broccoli. Can I call you that?” Simeon asked.
“No.”

“Got it. Here’s the thing. Kenzi here got a big heart. But that big heart happens to be in a small body. Now, I don’t know about you, but I would hate for that heart to be broken because that body was knocked around. That would be a tragesty.”
What are the explicit and implicit meanings of Simeon calling Ms. Wockley “Wockley Broccoli”?
What are the explicit and implicit meanings of the way Ms. Wockley says, “No”? What does it tell us about her relationship with Simeon and Kenzi?
Based on this dialogue, what do you think Ms. Wockley thinks about Simeon and Kenzi?
What does this type of explicit and implicit language tell us about how stories, and especially dialogue, can help us see through someone else’s eyes?
Pulse Check

In section 2 of “Five Things Easier to Do Than Simeon’s and Kenzi’s Secret Handshake,” Ms. Wockley asks, “Is that true, Mr. Thompson, that the hallways are scary for you?” What does this tell the reader about how Ms. Wockley sees the two boys?
She disapproves of their behavior, but she’s genuinely concerned for Kenzi.
She is skeptical of their excuses, but she comes to believe they are true.
She believes their excuses, but she cannot make an exception to the rules.
She admires their friendship, but she is angry that they are lying to her.
Part B: Dialogue Reveals Characters
Directions:

In your group, each person will become the expert on one piece of dialogue from this vignette. As you read your line, think about its explicit meaning, or what it says directly, and its implicit meaning, or what it suggests without saying it outright. Then use both of those meanings to figure out what the dialogue reveals about the character. As a group, you’ll share your thinking and record your ideas on the graphic organizer.
Jigsaw Reading

At the top of the three columns, label the first one ‘Quotes and Explicit Meanings,’ the second one ‘Implicit Meanings,’ and the third one ‘What Each Reveals About the Speaker.’ If your chart is already labeled, just take a moment to look at those headings so you know how we’ll use each column.
The conflict with Fredo in section 4, from “You made me lose count, man!” until the end of that section
The discussion after the conflict, from the beginning of section 5 through “. . . offered Simeon some”
The conversation around wishes in section 5, from “Happy birthday” through the repetition of “brothers”
Share at least one sentence from your excerpt with the rest of your group. Then share what you learned from at least one other group member.
How does the end of “Five Things Easier to Do Than Simeon’s and Kenzi’s Secret Handshake” give new meaning to why Simeon and Kenzi consider themselves brothers?
Reflection
Reflect on your understanding of how dialogue can reveal a point of view using the
Reflection
routine.
How confident are you in your ability to understand what dialogue tells us about a character’s point of view?
Reflection
What do you think Kenzi wished for? What has he said or done in the story that makes you think this?
Have students take out their copies of
Look Both Ways
. Share the following dialogue samples from Vignette 6 where all students can see them.
Say these Directions:
Look at the following dialogue samples for Vignette 6. We are going to discuss whether the samples are informative, entertaining, or both.
“Fantana banana, what’s good? What’s hood? What’s new? What’s true?”
“Anyway, like I was saying. We family.”
“To your mother’s house. Ask her how many times she dropped you when you were a baby.”
Informally poll the class on whether each sample dialogue is informational, entertaining, or both.
Ask:
Is the first dialogue sample informational, entertaining, or both? Tell us why.

The first one is both. It is entertaining because his language is funny, especially because he’s talking to a teacher who sounds very serious. It’s also informational because it shows the reader that Simeon is charming and a little silly but also respectful.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:

Today, we’re going to take a close look at the dialogue in “Five Things Easier to Do Than Simeon’s and Kenzi’s Secret Handshake” and discuss how it helps develop the characters, their relationship, and the story.
Students will complete a poll on whether they think three snippets of dialogue from this vignette are informative, entertaining, or both to prepare them to analyze dialogue throughout the lesson.
Language Study
Target Words:
explicit, implicit
Review the Words:
In Write or project the words explicit and implicit where all students can see them. Remind students that they studied these words in Lesson 5 and learned how they are related.
Ask:
Where have you seen the words
explicit
and
implicit
before? Do you remember how they are related?
Identify the Relationship Between the Words:
Review the relationship between the two words, and relate it to how students will explore explicit and implicit meanings in today’s lesson.
Say these Directions:
Explicit
and
implicit
are opposites.
Explicit
means “made clear with no room for confusion,” and
implicit
means “only implied or suggested.” Today, when we talk about the
explicit
and
implicit
meanings of words or phrases, we’re talking about what the exact words mean versus what they might imply in the context of this story.
Discuss Explicit and Implicit Meanings:

Lead a discussion about the explicit and implicit meanings of this piece of dialogue: “Mr. Cross, Mr. Thompson was just on your back yelling yee-haw while circling his arm in the air as if winding an imaginary lasso.” Remind students of its context: the teacher caught Kenzi riding on Simeon’s back in the hallway, they denied it, and now she’s explaining what she saw.
Ask:
Remember the context here: Kenzi was riding on Simeon’s back in the hallway. Ms. Wockley caught them, and they said they weren’t pretending to be in a horse race. What is the
explicit
meaning of what she says to them?
The explicit meaning is, “I saw one of you pretending to be a rodeo rider on the other.”
Ask:
What is the
implicit
meaning of what Ms. Wockley said?
The implicit meaning is, “Are you seriously going to pretend I don’t see the ridiculousness that is right in front of me?”
Ask:
Why would an author choose to use dialogue that is more
implicit
Implicit dialogue is more genuine, since it is a more natural way for people to talk. This helps make the dialogue more interesting to read and makes the characters more relatable as real people.
Help students name the explicit meaning of a line of dialogue and then infer the implicit meaning, using inference verbs and a short quoted phrase as evidence.
Teach a 2-step routine: (1) “Explicit = what the words say.” (2) “Implicit = what the speaker is really doing/feeling.”
After each student response, press for evidence by asking: “Which exact words made you think that?”
Model one complete response using the frame “Explicitly, ___. Implicitly, ___. This suggests ___ because ___.”
“Explicitly, the speaker says ___.”
“Implicitly, this suggests ___.”
“I think this reveals ___ because the line says, ‘___.’”
“The words ‘___’ make me think ___.”

Validate home language and community discourse knowledge by inviting students to connect to how tone/sarcasm works in real conversations, then return to the text: “Where do you hear that tone in the words?”
Upgrade “It’s funny/mean” → “The line implies ___ because the speaker ___.”
Turn vague inferences into text-based ones: “She’s annoyed” → “Her short reply implies impatience.”
If students give only a summary → Prompt: “Now add an implicit meaning using implies/suggests.”
If students give an inference with no evidence → Prompt: “Quote 2–5 words that support your idea.”
Students state one explicit meaning accurately.
Students state one implicit meaning using an inference verb (implies/suggests).
Students cite a short quoted phrase as evidence.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
Today, we are going to continue to analyze the dialogue in “Five Things Easier to Do Than Simeon’s and Kenzi’s Secret Handshake,” looking for
explicit
and
implicit
meanings in the story dialogue to discuss how this helps develop the characters, their relationship, and their story.
Students will review the terms
explicit
and
implicit
to identify explicit and implicit meanings in a given text.
Part A: Explicit and Implicit Meanings in Dialogue:
Look Both Ways
, Vignette 6 (RL.6.6, L.6.5)
(15 minutes)

This section focuses on deepening students’ ability to distinguish between explicit and implicit meaning in dialogue and connect those meanings to character relationships. Students should move beyond identifying what is said to analyzing what is implied and how that shapes reader's understanding of characters. Emphasize the use of inference language (e.g., implies, suggests, reveals) and require students to ground their thinking in specific words from the text. This work builds directly toward RL.6.6 by helping students analyze how dialogue reveals point of view and relationships.
Say these Directions:
In this part, we will continue to analyze the dialogue between Simeon, Kenzi, and Ms. Wockley, teasing apart
explicit
and
implicit
meanings to understand how stories help us see through someone else’s eyes.
Teach
Lead an echo-read of the following section from “Five Things Easier to Do Than Simeon’s and Kenzi’s Secret Handshake.” Read each line aloud, and have students echo it back.
“See here’s the thing, Wockley Broccoli. Can I call you that?” Simeon asked.
“No.”

“Got it. Here’s the thing. Kenzi here got a big heart. But that big heart happens to be in a small body. Now, I don’t know about you, but I would hate for that heart to be broken because that body was knocked around. That would be a travesty.”

Explain that there are both explicit and implicit meanings to what both Simeon and Ms. Wockley say here. This dialogue can tell us important information about how these characters relate to each other.
Discussion
Discuss the explicit and implicit meanings contained in the previous dialogue and what they tell us about the relationship between the characters.
Ask:
What are the
explicit
and
implicit
meanings of Simeon calling Ms. Wockley “Wockley Broccoli”?

An explicit meaning is that he likes to call people by silly names. An implicit meaning is that he sees her as someone he can talk to casually, like a friend, even though she is a stern teacher. It shows how confident and charming Simeon is and how good their relationship is.
Ask:
What are the
explicit
and
implicit
meanings of the way Ms. Wockley says, “No”? What does it tell us about her relationship with Simeon and Kenzi?

An explicit meaning is that she is simply saying, “No.” An implicit meaning is that she feels the need to act a little serious with them, but she is also willing to tolerate their goofiness and hear them out. She says no instead of just laughing or saying yes, but she also lets them keep explaining when she could just punish them and move on. It shows that their relationship is both fun and serious.
Ask:
Based on this dialogue, what do you think Ms. Wockley thinks about Simeon and Kenzi?

While she gets kind of annoyed with them, she also finds them charming and entertaining and wants to hear what they have to say. Earlier in this vignette, the narrator says, “She’d heard their excuse . . . but they were always so entertaining that she was game to hear it once more.” She reinforces this when she says no to the silly nickname but lets them keep talking and eventually lets them go with just a warning.
Ask:
What does this type of
explicit
and
implicit
language tell us about how stories, and especially dialogue, can help us see through someone else’s eyes?

This scene shows how explicit dialogue advances the story by creating authentic conversations. It can also reveal what another character is thinking by telling the story from multiple points of view. We know that Mr. Fantana has a soft spot for Simeon and the other students, even when they bother him, but we might think Ms. Wockley doesn’t like them at all. The implicit dialogue in this scene shows that even someone who is stern and serious can be charmed by them because they are so funny, witty, and kind. It shows how the relationship between teacher and student is important to all of them.
Ask:
Think about a time you said something to a friend or family member where the
implicit
meaning was very different from the
explicit
words. How does understanding that experience help you understand what these characters are doing?
Support students in explaining how dialogue reveals relationships by linking (a) what is said, (b) what is meant, and (c) what that shows about trust, power, or closeness between characters.
Invite multiple valid interpretations as long as they’re evidence-based: “Two readers can infer differently—both must prove it with the line.”
Require “relationship language” in responses (e.g., close, protective, tense, respectful, playful).
After students identify implicit meaning, ask: “So what does that show about their relationship?”
“This suggests their relationship is ___ because ___.”
“The speaker’s word choice implies ___, which reveals ___ (closeness/tension/respect).”
“The dialogue reveals ___ by showing ___.”
Model a “because” chain: implicit meaning → relationship → evidence.
Convert “They’re friends” → “Their playful teasing suggests closeness because ___.”
Replace general labels with relational traits: nice → supportive/protective/patient.
If students name only the implicit meaning → Prompt: “Add ‘This reveals their relationship is . . .’”
If students overgeneralize (“Teachers are always . . .”) → Prompt: “Stay in the vignette: What does Ms. Wockley do here?”
Students use relationship language (close/protective/tense/respectful).
Students use an inference verb (implies/suggests/reveals).
Students connect the inference to a quoted phrase from the excerpt.
Teacher Tip

Remind students how context can change the implicit meaning of some word choices. Ask them how calling a teacher by a goofy name may have a different result than calling a friend or relative by the same name. The fact that a character would say something to a teacher that would normally only be said to a friend has an implicit meaning.

content.text: Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Interpreting implicit meanings

If students struggle with identifying implicit meanings in dialogue, try comparing how it would read if it were slightly different, with a focus on what the difference would imply rather than the literal difference in meaning. Ex. “Imagine if, instead of saying ‘No,’ Ms. Wockley had given them a hard stare and started to write them up. Her answer would still be ‘No,’ but how would the implicit meaning of her response change? What do readers learn when Ms. Wockley chooses to engage with the boys?”
Ready for extension: Implicit meanings
Say:
Imagine what Simeon was going to say when he asked to make one more point. If possible, write dialogue that includes
implicit

meaning. He would say something like, “We’re all here to get an education, right? And we all want our equal rights, right? So I’m out here in the halls trying to educate everyone on the importance of watching out for the little guy!” The
implicit
meaning is that he knows what’s important to Ms. Wockley and how to charm her by speaking her language.
Pulse Check (RL.6.6)

In section 2 of “Five Things Easier to Do Than Simeon’s and Kenzi’s Secret Handshake,” Ms. Wockley asks, “Is that true, Mr. Thompson, that the hallways are scary for you?” What does this tell the reader about how Ms. Wockley sees the two boys?
She disapproves of their behavior, but she’s genuinely concerned for Kenzi.
Correct: The implicit meaning of her words is that she is genuinely concerned that Kenzi is afraid to walk the halls.
She is skeptical of their excuses, but she comes to believe they are true.
Incorrect: Ms. Wockley’s tone is sarcastic, and she is certainly skeptical, but she never believes that anything they say is true.
She believes their excuses, but she cannot make an exception to the rules.
Incorrect: She does not believe their excuses, but she lets them off with a warning anyway because she finds them so charming and entertaining.
She admires their friendship, but she is angry that they are lying to her.
Incorrect: Ms. Wockley makes it clear that she doesn’t believe them, but she isn’t angry and doesn’t exactly see what they say as lying.
Part B: Dialogue Reveals Characters (RL.6.6, L.6.5) (15 minutes)

Have students work in groups of three or four for this part of the lesson. Each student will become an expert on one piece of dialogue from this vignette by analyzing its explicit and implicit meanings to show what those meanings reveal about the character. Groups will work together to record findings on a graphic organizer.
Say these Directions:

In your group, each person will become the expert on one piece of dialogue from this vignette. As you read your line, think about its explicit meaning, or what it says directly, and its implicit meaning, or what it suggests without saying it outright. Then use both of those meanings to figure out what the dialogue reveals about the character. As a group, you’ll share your thinking and record your ideas on the graphic organizer.
Jigsaw Reading
Hand out copies of the
3 Column Chart graphic organizer
to each student. Label (or instruct them to label) the three columns “Quotes and Explicit Meanings,” “Implicit Meanings,” and “What Each Reveals About the Speaker.”
Say these Directions

At the top of the three columns, label the first one ‘Quotes and Explicit Meanings,’ the second one ‘Implicit Meanings,’ and the third one ‘What Each Reveals About the Speaker.’ If your chart is already labeled, just take a moment to look at those headings so you know how we’ll use each column.

Explain that each group member will become an expert on one piece of dialogue from this vignette. They will complete the organizer for their portion and share their thoughts with the rest of the group. Model filling out the information based on a sentence from a different part of the vignette.
Say:

Each person in your group is going to become an expert on one piece of dialogue from this vignette. That means you will focus on your assigned line, fill out the organizer for that part, and then share your thinking with the rest of your group so everyone can learn from one another. Before you start, I’m going to model how to fill in the organizer using a different sentence from another part of the vignette so you can see what this should look like.
Say:
If I am the expert for the passage where Ms. Wockley says, “I’m going to say this to you for the thousandth time,” I would say that the
explicit
meaning is that Ms. Wockley has told them before not to mess around in the hallway. The
implicit
meaning is that she is exhausted from having to repeat herself so many times. This tells us that the speaker is dealing with a lot at school and may not always feel heard or valued.
Assign each group member to one of the three excerpts listed below. Give them a few minutes to reread the section and add information to their graphic organizer.
The conflict with Fredo in section 4, from “You made me lose count, man!” until the end of that section
The discussion after the conflict, from the beginning of section 5 through “. . . offered Simeon some”
The conversation around wishes in section 5, from “Happy birthday” through the repetition of “brothers”
Say these Directions:
Take a few minutes to reread your excerpt and fill out the graphic organizer with at least one sentence from that section.
Excerpt 1, the conflict with Fredo in section 4
Quotes and Explicit Meanings
Implicit Meanings
What Each Reveals About the Speaker
“Where you gotta go, Fredo?” You don’t have anywhere else to be.
“To your mother’s house. Ask her how many times she dropped you when you were a baby.” I think something is wrong with you.
“She only dropped me once, into a vat of gold.” I’m obviously superior to you.
“And a vat of gravy.” You have always eaten a lot.
I like making fun of your job and implying it makes you a loser.
If you try to make fun of me, I’m going to make fun of you right back.
I can turn all your negatives into positives by being clever.
You’re fat.
He has a relationship with Fredo that involves a lot of good-natured teasing.
The relationship is two-sided, and Fredo participates too.
Their relationship can be kind of competitive, with each one trying to outdo the other.
Sometimes the line gets crossed, and one of them says something that’s actually hurtful.
When there are a few minutes remaining, instruct students to share their answers with the other members of their groups.
Say:
Share at least one sentence from your excerpt with the rest of your group. Then share what you learned from at least one other group member.

The member of my group who read the part about the conversation after leaving Fredo’s helped me understand both of them and their relationship better. They said that the way Kenzi made fun of Fredo had the implicit meaning that he wanted to defend Simeon from Fredo calling him fat. But Simeon saying, “But I can’t front, he got me with the gravy joke” showed that Simeon can take the joke. This also shows that while he’s not too bothered by it, he still appreciates Kenzi sticking up for him.
If time allows, discuss the following prompt as a large group.
Ask:
How does the end of “Five Things Easier to Do Than Simeon’s and Kenzi’s Secret Handshake” give new meaning to why Simeon and Kenzi consider themselves brothers?

We learn that Kenzi’s brother, Mason, went to jail for a crime that Simeon’s brother, Chucky, committed. They feel like brothers because their own brothers are bonded in this way. Simeon protects Kenzi like a big brother, just like Kenzi’s brother protected his. This shows that Simeon feels responsible for Kenzi’s brother being in jail. We also know that Kenzi misses his brother and feels sad about him. He does not seem to blame Simeon at all and has only gotten closer to him.

Support students in the Jigsaw Reading by helping them fill all three columns with precision: quote + explicit meaning, implicit meaning, and what it reveals about the speaker/relationship, using inference verbs and quoted evidence.
Provide a minimum requirement: 1 quote + 1 explicit meaning + 1 implicit meaning + 1 “reveals” statement per excerpt.
Remind students that implicit must go beyond repeating the explicit meaning.
During share-out, require peers to ask one clarification question (e.g., “What words made you think that?”).
Encourage academic inference verbs in columns 2–3: implies, suggests, indicates, reveals.
Push specificity in column 3: trait + relationship effect (e.g., “competitive teasing that sometimes crosses a line”).
Column 1: “The quote ‘___’ explicitly means ___.”
Column 2: “Implicitly, it suggests ___.”
Column 3: “This reveals the speaker is ___ and the relationship is ___ because ___.”
Allow students to draw on social knowledge of banter/roasting as a relationship practice, then anchor it back to the text (“Which line shows it’s playful vs. hurtful?”).
If column 2 is still literal → Prompt: “What is the speaker trying to do (protect, embarrass, deflect, impress)?”
If column 3 is vague (“He is funny”) → Prompt: “Funny how? Teasing to bond? Teasing to dominate? Use suggests/reveals + evidence.”
Students complete all three columns for at least one line of dialogue.
Students use at least one inference verb (implies/suggests/indicates/reveals).
Students include a short quote fragment to justify the inference.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Interpreting what dialogue reveals about characters

If students struggle with filling in the last column of the graphic organizer, try asking them specific questions about what is happening with that character in that scene. Ex. “How do you think the character feels here?” “How are their words making other characters feel?” “How would you describe them now that you’ve heard them say that?”
Ready for extension: Expanding how dialogue can reveal more about characters
Ask:

We saw how Kenzi was protective of Simeon when Fredo made fun of him. How might Fredo might make fun of Kenzi? How might Simeon respond? He could make fun of Kenzi by calling him “shrimp” or “short stuff.” Simeon would respond by just glaring at him really hard until he apologized.
Reflection
Reflect on your understanding of how dialogue can reveal a point of view using the
Reflection
routine.
How confident are you in your ability to understand what dialogue tells us about a character’s point of view?
Part A: Explicit and Implicit Meanings in Dialogue (RL.6.6, L.6.5)
Students will echo-read another excerpt from this vignette to discuss the explicit and implicit meanings within it and how such meanings reveal characters and their points of view.
Part B: Dialogue Reveals Characters (RL.6.6, L.6.5)

Students will perform a Jigsaw Reading to become an expert on one of three selected excerpts of dialogue from the vignette, analyzing explicit and implicit meanings and what they reveal about the speakers.

This reflection provides an opportunity for students to synthesize their understanding of how dialogue and actions reveal character perspective. Students should use evidence from across the vignette—not just a single moment—to support their inferences. Encourage students to connect implicit meaning to larger character motivations and relationships, reinforcing the lesson’s focus on point of view and empathy.
Reflection
Prompt students to reflect on today’s lesson by writing a brief response to the following prompt.
Ask:
What do you think Kenzi wished for? What has he said or done in the story that makes you think this?

The last paragraphs tell us that Simeon knows that Kenzi wants to carry a message to his brother to tell him how much he misses him. I think Kenzi also wishes to have his brother free again, and for Simeon not to blame himself. I know this because we see at the end how much Kenzi misses his brother, and throughout the story, we also see that Kenzi loves Simeon as a brother and doesn’t blame him for what happened. He probably wishes Simeon wouldn’t blame himself either.
Students will reflect on the vignette by speculating on what a character may have been thinking.
Instruct students to read the next vignette, “Satchmo’s Master Plan,” and take notes in their
Journal
on the following prompt:
How is the structure of this vignette similar to or different from others you’ve read so far?

standards.description: Explain how an author develops the point of view of the narrator or speaker in a text.
Use context (e.g., the overall meaning of a sentence or paragraph; a word’s position or function in a sentence) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
Use the relationship between particular words (e.g., cause/effect, part/whole, item/category) to better understand each of the words.
Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

By the end of the year, read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, in the grades 6–8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
Describe how a particular story’s or drama’s plot unfolds in a series of episodes as well as how the characters respond or change as the plot moves toward a resolution.

Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information and evidence, paraphrasing key ideas, building on responses, and providing useful feedback.
Engage in conversational exchanges and express ideas on familiar topics by asking and answering yes‐no and wh‐ questions and responding using simple phrases.
Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information, and paraphrasing key ideas.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations using appropriate register (e.g., to reflect on multiple perspectives) using a variety of learned phrases, indirect reported speech (e.g., I heard you say X, and Gabriel just pointed out Y), as well as open responses.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to gain and hold the floor or ask for clarification) using basic learned phrases (e.g., I think..., Would you please repeat that?), as well as open responses.
Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to provide counterarguments) using an expanded set of learned phrases (I agree with X, but...), as well as open responses.
Express inferences and conclusions drawn based on close reading of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia using a variety of precise academic verbs (e.g., indicates that, influences).
Express inferences and conclusions drawn based on close reading of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia using some frequently used verbs (e.g., shows that, based on).
Express inferences and conclusions drawn based on close reading of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia using a variety of verbs (e.g., suggests that, leads to).

content.text: How do ordinary moments reveal who we are and how we belong?
